name: Neutrons
kicker: The neutral particle in the nucleus · Key to isotopes and chain reactions
briefing: Neutrons are the uncharged particles packed into the nucleus of almost every atom alongside protons, and each one is just slightly heavier than a proton. James Chadwick discovered them in 1932. Changing the number of neutrons makes a different isotope of the same element, and neutrons trigger nuclear chain reactions: when one splits a uranium-235 nucleus, two or three more fly out to split others.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1930, Walther Bothe [“BOH-tuh”] and Herbert Becker found that beryllium struck by alpha particles gave off a penetrating radiation that was really a stream of these particles. Irène Joliot-Curie [“ee-REN zhoh-LYOH kyoo-REE”] and Frédéric Joliot then saw that radiation knock protons out of paraffin wax, but they mistook it for gamma rays.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles discovered by James Chadwick in 1932.

tossups.p: In 1920, Ernest Rutherford predicted that atomic nuclei held a neutral particle about as heavy as a proton. Twelve years later, a scientist working under him at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge proved that these particles exist.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles discovered by James Chadwick, which have no electric charge.

tossups.p: Outside an atom’s nucleus, one of these particles lasts only about 15 minutes on average before the weak force makes it decay into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino. That process is called beta decay.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that sit alongside protons in the nucleus.

tossups.p: Physicists who trap these particles in a “bottle” and physicists who count their decays in a “beam” get average lifetimes that disagree by about nine seconds, a long-standing puzzle. That lifetime matters for working out how much helium formed after the Big Bang.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles found in atomic nuclei, discovered in 1932.

tossups.p: In 1933, while waiting to cross a street in London, Leo Szilard [“SIL-ard”] imagined a chain reaction in which each atom that splits releases more of these particles. Szilard later patented that idea in Britain.
tossups.r: A uranium-235 nucleus that splits releases two or three of them. For 10 points, name these neutral particles that drive nuclear chain reactions.

tossups.p: Enrico Fermi found that these particles work far better at making elements radioactive after they are slowed down by passing through paraffin wax. Nuclear reactors use moderators such as graphite or heavy water to slow these particles down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that, along with protons, make up atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: Boron’s isotope with mass number 10 is especially good at absorbing these particles. Control rods made of boron or cadmium soak up these particles to keep a nuclear reactor’s chain reaction from running out of control.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these uncharged particles found in the nucleus, which were discovered by James Chadwick.

tossups.p: Even though these particles have no electric charge, each one has a magnetic moment, a sign that it is built from smaller charged pieces. Those pieces are one up quark and two down quarks, whose charges add up to zero.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles found in atomic nuclei, about as heavy as protons but with no charge.

tossups.p: Clifford Shull and Bertram Brockhouse won the 1994 Nobel Prize in Physics for bouncing beams of these particles off solids and liquids to learn how their atoms are arranged and how they move. Because these particles have no charge, they slip deep into materials.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that share the nucleus with protons.

tossups.p: A few minutes after the Big Bang, about one of these particles remained for every seven protons, and nearly all of them ended up inside helium nuclei. Each helium-4 nucleus contains two of these particles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles discovered by James Chadwick in 1932.

tossups.p: The common isotope lead-208 holds a “magic” number of these particles, 126, which makes its nucleus especially stable. Heavy stable nuclei like that one contain more of these particles than protons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles whose number differs among isotopes of the same element.

tossups.p: The collapsed cores of some exploded stars, only about 20 kilometers across, are made mostly of these particles, which resist being squeezed together because of the Pauli exclusion principle. That resistance, called degeneracy pressure, keeps such cores from collapsing further.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that join protons in atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: Cosmic rays striking the upper atmosphere knock loose these particles, which turn nitrogen atoms into carbon-14 for radiocarbon dating. Carbon-14 has eight of these particles, two more than ordinary carbon-12.
tossups.r: An atom’s count of them equals its mass number minus its atomic number. For 10 points, name these neutral particles.

tossups.p: Ordinary hydrogen is the only stable kind of atom with none of these particles, while its isotope deuterium has one and radioactive tritium has two. Heavy water, made with deuterium, is used to slow these particles down in some nuclear reactors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that, with protons, make up the nucleus.

tossups.p: In 1956, physicists at Berkeley’s Bevatron accelerator discovered the antiparticle of these particles. The scientist who first identified these particles won the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics and later led Britain’s team on the Manhattan Project.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these uncharged particles, slightly heavier than protons, that James Chadwick discovered in 1932.

trap.title: Neutron, not neutrino
trap.body: The names sound alike because Wolfgang Pauli first called his ghostly particle a “neutron” before Enrico Fermi renamed it the neutrino, or “little neutral one,” after Chadwick found the much heavier neutron in 1932. Both have no electric charge, so “neutral” alone won’t tell you which one a tossup wants, and neutron stars are a separate answer line too.
trap.fix: The nucleus, isotopes, Chadwick, chain reactions, moderators, and control rods mean neutrons. Ghost particles, the Sun, oscillation, Super-Kamiokande, and IceCube mean neutrinos. A whole collapsed star about 20 kilometers across means neutron star.
trap.line: Real answer line: neutrons (prompt on nucleons, baryons, or hadrons; do not accept “neutrinos”)
